area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain and demonstrate from the right seat a soft-field approach and landing at the approach speed ±5 knots, touching down at the slowest possible speed with the nose wheel held off, and you can set up safe soft-field practice and spot and fix the errors learners make.
why: The soft-field landing asks a learner to do things a normal landing taught them not to do: keep power on in the flare, keep the nose up after touchdown, and keep rolling instead of braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Old habits fight new ones, so this is a lesson about habit as much as stick and rudder [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. It is also flown slow and close to the ground, the part of a flight where the margin of safety is smallest [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

warmup: Think first: your learner flies a perfect normal landing, then on the next pattern, briefed for a soft-field landing, chops the power over the numbers and drops the nose wheel onto the runway. Do they not know the procedure, or did an old habit win? What would you ask, and what would you watch for on the next approach, to tell the difference?

key_terms.def: A landing on snow, sand, mud, tall grass or a rough surface, made as smoothly as possible at the slowest possible speed, with the wings carrying the weight as long as practical [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Moving the airplane's weight from the wings to the wheels after touchdown. Back-elevator pressure and engine power control its rate [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Reduced induced drag close to the surface. It is 'borrowed' performance that is repaid when the airplane climbs out of it [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Altitude and speed are off in the same direction (lower and slower, or higher and faster). Corrected with the throttle [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Altitude and speed are off in opposite directions (higher and slower, or lower and faster). Corrected with the elevator [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Slow flight where more power is needed to fly slower. A low-speed, high-pitch power approach is flown here [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
How much the gusts exceed the steady wind. With no manufacturer speed, add no more than one-half of it to 1.3 VSO [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
The airplane climbs during the round out because pitch and angle of attack were raised too fast [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
Weight concentrated on the nose wheel during the roll, so the airplane swerves or pivots on it [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].
When learning one skill hinders learning another [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
The runway distance available to land and stop before a LAHSO hold-short point, published in the Chart Supplement [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

chunks.title: The maneuver and the standard you are held to

body.p: Purpose: on soft or rough surfaces such as snow, sand, mud or tall grass, the goal is to touch down as smoothly as possible at the slowest possible speed. The wings carry the weight as long as practical, which protects the gear on a rough surface and keeps the wheels from sinking into a soft one [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

Procedure in one breath: a normal-looking approach at the short-field approach speed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]; some power held through the level-off and touchdown while the airplane flies 1 to 2 feet up in ground effect [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]; touchdown nose-high at the lowest possible speed; nose wheel held off; no brakes; keep moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Normal approach and landing basics (aim point, round out, the normal touchdown) are taught in lesson AI.VII.B. This lesson only covers what changes on a soft field, and how you teach those changes.

Kept off the surface until loss of elevator effectiveness (ACS PA.IV.D.S9)

Your extra job
None
Demonstrate and explain at the same time, and analyze and correct common errors (ACS AI.VII.D Skills, S14)

callout.text: The AFM/POH speeds, flap settings and procedures come first. If the AFH differs from the manufacturer, the manufacturer's recommendations take precedence [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

check.q: Your learner's POH gives 61 knots for a short-field approach. What window applies to them on the private checkride, and to you on the CFI checkride?
check.a: Learner: 56 to 71 knots (+10/-5, ACS PA.IV.D.S7). You: 56 to 66 knots (±5, ACS AI.VII.D.S7). The soft-field landing uses the short-field approach speed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

chunks.title: Energy on a slow final: the stabilized approach

body.p: Stabilized approach: a constant-angle glide path toward a chosen point, at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Set pitch, power and trim right after rolling out on final, then make only small corrections [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. On a soft field there is no reason for a steep angle unless obstacles are present [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

Energy management concepts: altitude and speed are two stores of one total energy. If both are off the same way (lower and slower), total energy is wrong and the throttle fixes it. If they are off opposite ways (lower and faster), only the distribution is wrong and the elevator trades one for the other. Mixed errors need both controls together [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

Why this matters more on a soft field: you fly the slow short-field approach speed, near the left column of Figure 4-12. A low-speed, high-pitch power approach sits in the region of reversed command. If sink builds, power can stop it; lowering the nose without power gives a fast sink [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. The AFH lists unstable or slow approaches as one way pilots run out of energy with no way back [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

bullets: Low on final: add power and raise the nose together to hold airspeed, then rejoin the path. Never raise the nose alone and never retract flaps [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].
Stretching the glide with pitch alone raises angle of attack, bleeds airspeed and can end in a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Slow on final: the learner cannot judge sink rate or round-out height. Add power early; too slow and too low means go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].
Speed target: the POH speed, or no more than 1.3 VSO plus no more than half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Extra speed only floats you in ground effect [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

callout.text: Teaching tip: when the learner is low and slow, ask 'which store is empty?' before they touch anything. Saying 'total energy, throttle' out loud builds the right reflex for a slow final.

check.q: Short final to grass: you are 20 feet low and 5 knots fast. Throttle, elevator or both?
check.a: Elevator first. Lower and faster is an energy distribution error: ease back to trade the extra speed for height, keeping the throttle where it is [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

chunks.title: Power in the flare and the slowest possible touchdown

body.p: The one big difference from a normal landing: a degree of power stays on through the level-off and touchdown. That lets airspeed bleed off slowly while the airplane flies 1 to 2 feet off the surface, so the wings still hold much of the weight when the wheels first touch. This cuts the nose-over force at touchdown [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

bullets: Elevator authority: a small amount of power blows more air over the elevator, so the learner can still flare at low speed. A windmilling propeller at idle can block that airflow [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Ground effect itself reduces elevator effectiveness and makes the nose harder to raise [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]. Expect more back pressure than in a normal flare.

Power adds lift without more angle of attack and slows the sink. If the learner is in the landing attitude and slightly high, hold the attitude and add a little power to ease down [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].
Closing the throttle too rapidly can cause an immediate jump in sink rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Touchdown is made at the lowest possible airspeed in a nose-high attitude [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

body.p: Ballooning (Figure 9-34) is the error to expect when a learner raises the nose too fast in this long, slow float. The airplane climbs while speed decays toward a stall. A little power cushions a small balloon; a big one means go around, with power applied before the stall [[24:203|AFH 9-32]] [[24:204|AFH 9-33]].

Minimum sink rate is the point of S10. A 6-inch free fall is roughly a 340 fpm descent, and touchdown loads can reach three or four times the airplane's weight [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. On a soft surface that load goes straight into wheels that can dig in.

callout.text: Pitch holds the picture, power sets the sink. Say it on every soft-field demo until the learner says it back.

check.q: Your learner holds the soft-field float nicely, then pulls the throttle to idle a foot above the grass. What will you likely see, and why?
check.a: A sudden sink and a hard touchdown, maybe nose wheel first. Closing the throttle quickly raises the sink rate [[24:193|AFH 9-22]], and at idle the elevator loses the propeller airflow it needs to hold the nose up [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

chunks.title: Nose wheel off: weight transfer, rollout and taxi

body.p: After the mains touch, hold enough back-elevator pressure to keep the nose wheel off. Back pressure and power together control how fast the weight moves from wings to wheels [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The S9 standard is to keep the nose wheel off until loss of elevator effectiveness (ACS AI.VII.D.S9). The AFH uses the same idea for the short-field landing: hold the pitch attitude as long as the elevators remain effective [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

bullets: Once committed to landing, lower the nose wheel gently. A slight addition of power usually helps ease it down [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
On a very poor surface, the mains may just touch while the wings carry the weight until a suitable taxi surface is reached [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
No brakes. Braking loads the nose gear and can make the nose wheel dig in; the soft surface slows the airplane by itself [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Leave the flaps down on the rollout. Full control matters more than cleaning up [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Exit the soft area with enough speed: on a very soft field more power may be needed just to keep moving and not get stuck [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

body.p: Wheelbarrowing is the opposite of what you want. Weight on the nose wheel at speed lets the airplane swerve or pivot on it, especially in a crosswind. Its most common cause is touching down on all three wheels too fast and then pushing forward on the yoke [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

Taxiing on the soft surface: keep the airplane in continuous motion with sufficient power, because stopping on mud or snow can bog it down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. It takes more power to start moving than to keep moving [[24:56|AFH 2-19]]. Hold the controls for the wind: quartering headwind, upwind aileron up; quartering tailwind, elevator down and upwind aileron down [[24:56|AFH 2-19]].

Tailwheel airplanes: the tailwheel touches with or just before the mains and firm back-elevator pressure holds it down the whole roll, with no brakes and maybe more power [[24:294|AFH 14-8]]. The S9 nose wheel clause applies to tricycle gear.

callout.text: Exit plan: at a towered field leave at the first available taxiway and do not stop or reverse course on the runway without ATC approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]. Brief where firm ground is before you land.

check.q: S11 says to hold the elevator 'as recommended by manufacturer' on the rollout. If the POH says nothing, what does the AFH technique give you?
check.a: Enough back pressure to keep the nose wheel off, then a gentle lowering once committed, eased with a little power [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Then keep moving to firm ground.

chunks.title: Atmosphere, weight, surface and the landing numbers

body.p: Effects of atmospheric conditions: thin air does not change the indicated speed you land at, but true airspeed is higher, so the roll is longer. Minimum landing distance at 5,000 feet is 16 percent greater than at sea level, about 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

head: Change
Effect on landing distance
Source
rows: 10% more weight
About 5% faster landing speed and 10% more distance
Tailwind of 10 knots
About 21% more distance
10% excess landing speed
At least 21% more distance
Upsloping runway
Usually a shorter landing roll
Downsloping runway

Snow, ice or soft ground

body.p: Tailwind: the airplane lands at the same airspeed, so a tailwind raises groundspeed at touchdown, and the effect of wind on deceleration is just as large [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Application: on a soft field you also give up the brakes, so all of that extra ground speed has to be absorbed by the surface.

Runway surface/condition: chart data usually assume paved, level, smooth and dry. Surfaces vary from concrete to gravel, dirt or grass, and the Chart Supplement lists each one [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Mud and water reduce tire friction but can also act as obstructions that shorten the landing [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Slope and surface for an airport are both in the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

callout.text: Some AFMs give little or no guidance on correcting takeoff and landing distance for contaminated runways [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Teach learners to notice when the book is silent and to add margin, not to assume the paved number.

check.q: A learner plans a grass strip landing at max weight with a 10-knot tailwind 'because it's easier traffic.' Which two items from the table stack against them?
check.a: The tailwind adds about 21% [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]] and the extra weight also adds distance, 10% per 10% weight [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]], on top of the soft surface's significant effect.

chunks.title: Crosswind and gusts at the slowest speed

body.p: Wind correction techniques: the wing-low (sideslip) method keeps the ground track and longitudinal axis on the centerline through round out, touchdown and rollout, so no side load hits the gear [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. Rudder aligns the nose; aileron sets just enough bank to stop the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

Crosswind on a soft field: the soft-field technique makes the crosswind job harder. As airspeed decays in the round out, the controls become less effective and the correction you were holding becomes too small, so deflection has to increase gradually [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. A long, slow float at the lowest possible speed is exactly that situation, held for longer. Touchdown comes on the upwind main wheel first [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

bullets: If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn at the bank you need, the wind is too strong for that runway [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Certification shows control in 90° crosswinds up to 0.2 VSO [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].
With nose-wheel steering linked to the rudder, relax the rudder correction as the nose wheel touches, or the airplane swerves [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
On the rollout, more and more aileron goes into the wind as speed drops; full aileron into the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
Gusts: pilots often add half the gust factor; with a 70-knot approach and 15-knot gusts, 77 knots is appropriate. Partial flaps give more positive control in gusty crosswinds [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

callout.text: After a balloon the airplane is slower, so the crosswind pushes it more and the wing has to go lower still. If there is any doubt or it starts to drift, go around [[24:204|AFH 9-33]].

check.q: Halfway through the soft-field float your learner's drift starts again even though they have not moved the controls. Why?
check.a: Speed is decaying, so the same control deflection gives less correction. They must gradually add aileron and rudder to keep the wing down and the nose straight [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

chunks.title: Choosing the strip and the touchdown point

body.p: Selection of runway: landings become more hazardous as the calculated distance approaches the runway available [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Weigh four things: pilot capability, airplane performance and limitations, available distance, and wind (ACS AI.VII.D.R1).

bullets: Pilot capability: personal minimums come from experience. If a pilot has never used a runway shorter than 5,000 feet, their shortest-runway minimum is 5,000 feet [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. The same honesty applies to grass and mud.
Unfamiliar airport: add at least 500 feet to the runway-length minimum [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].
Airplane: approach speed, flaps and corrections from the POH [[24:172|AFH 9-1]]; in a low-wing airplane mud, stones or slush can damage the flaps [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Distance and wind: use the POH charts and the surface and slope from the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

body.p: Look before you land: the AIH says to teach pre-landing reconnaissance of unfamiliar or uncontrolled fields [[25:193|AIH 10-9]], and the PHAK suggests an aerial visual inspection of unfamiliar airports when possible [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

Aim and touchdown points: do not teach them mechanically. The learner picks them from the aircraft type, the landing being attempted, the conditions and the expected performance [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Application: on a soft strip that means aiming so the slow touchdown lands on the firmest, smoothest part, not just past the numbers.

Grass strips are often narrow and sloped. A narrower-than-usual runway or an upsloping runway makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly a lower approach [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Teach learners to check the altimeter often and to read slope from the Chart Supplement before they go [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

callout.text: Wrong surface landings happen. Verify alignment and runway number on every final; if in doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

check.q: Your learner has 60 hours, all on 5,000-foot paved runways, and wants to land on a 2,400-foot turf strip solo next week. What does the RMH approach to personal minimums say?
check.a: Their shortest-runway minimum should reflect what they have actually done, so 5,000 feet [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. Lower it one variable at a time, with training from an instructor first [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]: dual turf landings with you.

body.p: Windshear: a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a small area, worst close to the ground. A headwind changing to a tailwind drops airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On approach, a microburst can force the airplane to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

Why it bites harder here: the soft-field approach is flown at the slow short-field speed with no more than half the gust factor added [[24:192|AFH 9-21]], close to the 'very slow' cautions of Figure 4-12 [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. Application: a sudden airspeed loss leaves little room. Brief a go-around with full power at the first sign of a shear, and skip the lesson near convective weather.

head: Wake situation
What to do
rows: Landing behind a larger aircraft, same runway
Stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point, land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Landing behind a larger aircraft departing the same runway
Note its rotation point and land well before it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
After a larger aircraft's low approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes before landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]

body.p: Wake turbulence and the soft-field touchdown (application): 'land beyond its touchdown point' may put you past the firm part of a soft strip, or leave too little room for a no-brake rollout. If you cannot do both, wait or pick another runway.

Tailwind: a tailwind can move a preceding aircraft's vortices forward into the touchdown zone, and the light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. It also adds about 21% to landing distance at 10 knots [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

check.q: Why can 'land beyond the larger aircraft's touchdown point' be a poor fit for a soft-field landing?
check.a: Landing beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] can put the slow, no-brake touchdown past the firm part of the strip or leave too little room to roll. If both can't be met, wait or choose another runway.

body.p: Rejected landing and go-around: a go-around is a normal maneuver, and any approach may end in one. Delay comes from landing expectancy and from pride [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Teach it as part of every soft-field lesson, not as a failure.

bullets: The soft-field landing keeps the go-around door open longer: until the weight is on the wheels and the nose wheel is down, full power and a takeoff are still possible, if obstacles and field length allow [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
From the float you are slow and in ground effect. Full power smoothly; don't pitch up for a climb below the speed the airplane can climb at [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Ground effect performance is borrowed. Climbing out too early may leave the airplane unable to climb at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Retract flaps in small steps. A sudden full retraction can settle the airplane into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
A very low go-around may touch the runway again. That is not dangerous if the airplane is kept straight at a safe pitch attitude [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: Land and hold short operations (LAHSO): you may accept a LAHSO clearance only if you can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]. Student pilots and pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate, and the PIC has the final authority to decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. A LAHSO clearance does not rule out a rejected landing [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

callout.text: Application: practicing soft-field landings on a paved runway means a long float and a no-brake rollout. That uses more runway than a normal landing, so it is a poor match for a hold-short clearance. Decline LAHSO for this lesson, and say so on the radio before the clearance is issued if you can [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

check.q: Name the two causes of go-around delay the AFH gives, and how each could show up on a soft-field lesson.
check.a: Landing expectancy (assuming the long float will work out) and pride (seeing a go-around as failure) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Tell learners any approach may end in a go-around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

body.p: Collision hazards: in a study of midair collisions, flight instructors were on board in 37 percent of them, and most happened at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Many soft strips are nontowered. If learners think you do all the scanning, they never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

bullets: Radio: say the airport name at the start and end of each call, use the runway number, never 'active runway' [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]], and report downwind, base and final [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].
Scan: check the runway and the area around it for traffic and obstructions (ACS AI.VII.D.S4), and take a moment on every final to verify the landing zone is the correct one [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Checklists: finish briefings and checklists before the approach, except the landing checklist, so attention stays on the approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Low altitude maneuvering, stall and spin: sixty percent of stall/spin accidents happened during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. A skidding cross-control stall is most likely in a poorly flown base-to-final turn that overshoots; the safest fix is a go-around, and banks over 30° and skidding turns are out [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. CFIT often follows flight at high density altitude, in mountainous terrain, at night, in low visibility, or flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]], all common around back-country strips.

Distractions and task prioritization: the margin of safety is smallest on approach and landing, where an emergency or distraction can overtax the pilot [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]. Many distractions start as a minor problem [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Your own coaching is a distraction too: too much talk on final hurts collision avoidance and situational awareness and causes missed calls, so use only concise prompts [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
Loss of situational awareness or disorientation: snow-covered or featureless terrain can make you feel higher than you are, the 'black hole' effect that leads to a low approach [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

check.q: On a soft-field lesson, the learner overshoots final at a grass strip and starts adding bottom rudder to swing the nose around. What do you call for?
check.a: A go-around. That is the setup for a skidding cross-control stall close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Most soft-field training, and most checkrides, happen on pavement. No source here gives a procedure for simulating a soft field. What the sources do give is how to build realistic, safe scenarios.

bullets: Make the scenario realistic but never one that pushes a learner into an unsafe attitude or speed [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Name the 'soft' part: 'treat the first 1,500 feet as wet grass; keep the nose up until we turn off.'

Watch drift and airspeed closely while the learner is in ground effect, and don't let drift grow past what they can control. The AIH says this about soft-field takeoffs [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; the same long float happens on the landing.

Be aware of the risk of slow flight and of anything that reduces safety margins [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Brief a firm go-around rule: any balloon you have to fix with big inputs, any drift, any floating past your chosen point.
Do all the teaching on the ground or before you call the tower or CTAF. The learner's attention is almost all on flying close to the ground [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Guard the controls. Anxious learners can be very strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], and a learner who suddenly drops the nose at low speed or slams in power is most likely here.

body.p: Rollout on pavement: have the learner hold the nose wheel off as long as the elevator is effective [[24:193|AFH 9-22]], lower it gently with a touch of power [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], and keep rolling to the taxiway without brakes, as if stopping would bog down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]. Make sure the runway ahead and the time spent on it allow that: exit without delay [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

Application: a good build-up is a few low passes along a long runway, holding the airplane 1 to 2 feet up with a little power while it slows, then a go-around. This is your own technique, not FAA text, so brief it, pick a long runway, and set the go-around point before you start.

callout.text: In any simulation, agree who has the throttle. For simulated emergency landings the AFH says either the instructor or the learner must have complete control of it [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; the same clarity prevents a split-second argument when the float goes wrong.

check.q: Why tell a learner exactly which part of a paved runway is 'soft' before the approach?
check.a: It makes the scenario realistic and gives a clear exit target, without pushing them into an unsafe attitude or speed [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. It also lets you check that the no-brake rollout fits the runway.

body.p: Build on slow flight. The AIH's own example of positive transfer is slow flight helping a learner learn short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]], and the soft-field landing flies the same slow approach speed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Expect negative transfer too (application): the normal-landing habits of idle power in the flare and lowering the nose after touchdown will try to come back. Correct habits are much easier to build from the start than to fix later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

head: Phase
In the soft-field lesson
rows: Phase I: stick and rudder
Power and airspeed management, configuration, pattern placement, wind correction, aim point and sight picture, repeated until solid [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
Phase II: the factors
On the ground: surface, slope, grass corrections, rejected landings, a short strip at high weight and density altitude [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
Phase III: the scenario
A cross-country that ends at a turf strip, with a realistic change that forces a decision [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]

body.p: Early on the learner is in the cognitive stage: performing takes all their attention and distractions make it fall apart, so give a clear step-by-step model first [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Keep the explanation short before they fly; specific comments mean more once they have partly mastered it [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

head: When
What you do
What you say (short)
rows: Short final
Hold the short-field speed and a constant angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
'Short-field speed, no steeper than we need.'
Level-off
Round out and leave some power in [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
'Power stays in. We fly it a foot or two up.'
Float
Raise the nose slowly as speed bleeds off [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
'Nose comes up as it slows, a little at a time.'
Touchdown
Mains touch at the lowest speed, nose high [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
'Mains on, nose stays up.'
Rollout
Back pressure, then lower the nose gently with a touch of power; no brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
'Feet off the brakes. Ease the nose down.'
Taxi
Keep moving to firm ground [[24:145|AFH 6-13]]
'Keep it rolling.'

body.p: Watch for a learning plateau after the first quick progress; it is normal. Over-practice can cause it, and a break to another task can help [[25:77|AIH 3-26]]. Ten soft-field landings in a row is rarely the answer.

check.q: Why is slow flight a good lesson to schedule just before the first soft-field landing?
check.a: It transfers positively: the AIH's example is slow flight helping a learner learn short-field landings [[25:91|AIH 3-40]], and the soft-field landing uses the same slow approach speed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

body.p: The first eight rows are the AFH's own list of soft-field errors [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The rest come from the AFH section on faulty landings. 'What you see' and 'fix' use the AFH text around each one.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Excessive descent rate on final
Steep picture, high sink, runway growing long and narrow
No steep angle without obstacles [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]; reduce sink early, go around if it is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Excessive airspeed on final
Fast over the threshold, long float
Fly the short-field approach speed; higher speeds float in ground effect [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Unstable approach
Big pitch and power changes on short final
Set pitch, power and trim right after rolling out; small corrections [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Round out too high
Airplane levels off high and slows
Hold the attitude until it starts to settle, with a little power; don't lower the nose without power [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Poor power management in round out and touchdown
Throttle chopped, or power left high so it floats
Some power through touchdown, adjusted to control sink and weight transfer [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Hard touchdown
Firm contact, maybe a bounce
Minimum sink: power cushions, no rapid throttle closing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]
Poor control of weight transfer
Nose drops early, or the airplane skips
Back pressure and power together set the rate [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Nose wheel allowed to fall
Nose wheel slaps down after touchdown
Keep back pressure, then lower it gently with a little power [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Ballooning in the float
Airplane climbs, speed decays
Small: hold attitude, add power. Large: go around [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]
Wheelbarrowing
Swerving on the nose wheel
Smooth back pressure; go around if runway permits [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]
Braking on the soft surface
Nose pitches down, nose wheel digs in
Feet off the brakes; the surface slows you [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]

body.p: On the checkride the examiner may fly as a learner and make one of these errors. Name what you see, say the likely cause (skill, or an old normal-landing habit), show the fix, and have them try again. Teach problems and solutions from what actually happened on that approach, not a memorized script [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

check.q: Your learner's touchdowns are smooth but the nose wheel always comes down hard a second later. Which AFH error is it, and what is your fix?
check.a: Allowing the nose wheel to 'fall' instead of controlling its descent [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Fix: keep back pressure after touchdown, then lower it gently with a slight addition of power [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-24. Soft/rough field approach and landing. (AFH 9-23)
f1.alt: An airplane descends on a blue glide path toward a dirt strip, levels off a little above the surface in a zone marked Ground effect, floats along it, and touches down nose-high in a smaller zone marked Transition area.

f2.caption: Figure 4-12. The control skills needed to correct total energy and energy distribution errors, with an added column of cautions for the 'very slow' condition. (AFH 4-13)
f2.alt: A grid with altitude (higher, desired, lower) down the side and airspeed (very slow cautions, slower, desired, faster) across the top. Each box gives the throttle and elevator action. The lower, very slow box says: Dangerous, apply full throttle, avoid pitching up when on the backside of the power required curve.

f3.caption: Figure 9-34. Ballooning during roundout. (AFH 9-33)
f3.alt: An airplane descends from the right toward runway 34, levels near the surface just past the threshold, then pitches up and climbs away from the runway in a nose-high attitude.

f4.caption: Figure 2-15. Control positions of the nosewheel airplane. (AFH 2-20)
f4.alt: Top view of an airplane in a circle split into four quarters, each with a wind arrow. Wind from the front quarters: up aileron on that wing and neutral elevator. Wind from the rear quarters: down aileron on that wing and down elevator.

f5.caption: Figure 17-7. Runway illusions. (PHAK 17-11)
f5.alt: Paired pictures. A narrower runway looks as if you are higher and leads to a lower approach; a wider runway does the opposite. A downsloping runway looks as if you are lower and leads to a higher approach; an upsloping runway leads to a lower approach. Dotted lines show the normal approach and red arrows the approach flown because of the illusion.

f6.caption: Figure 1-14. Accidents often occur when flying task requirements exceed pilot capabilities; the difference is the margin of safety, smallest during approach and landing. (AIH 1-26)
f6.alt: A ribbon chart over time from preflight, takeoff and cruise to approach and landing. The task requirements band rises steeply at approach and landing until it nearly meets the pilot capabilities band, squeezing the margin of safety between them.

f7.caption: Figure 9-30. Right and wrong methods of correction for low final approach. (AFH 9-30)
f7.alt: An airplane low on final. Right: (1) add power, nose up, hold altitude, then (2) intercept the normal glidepath and resume a normal approach. Wrong: dragging it in to the runway with high power and a high pitch attitude.

scenario.title: A learner's first real turf strip
scenario.setup: You are flying with a private pilot who wants a checkout for a 2,600-foot turf strip with a slight upslope, used by a glider club. They have only landed on long paved runways. It rained last night. Wind is a light quartering tailwind on the favored runway and a 9-knot crosswind on the other end. A towplane and glider are working the pattern, and there are building cumulus 20 miles west. Your learner wants to 'just get it done' because friends are waiting at the strip.

questions.q: Before you go, how do you decide whether this strip fits this pilot and this airplane today?
questions.a: Run the POH landing numbers with the surface and slope from the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]], knowing many AFMs give little guidance for wet or contaminated surfaces [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Compare with personal minimums built from real experience [[30:16|RMH 2-4]], plus at least 500 feet for an unfamiliar airport [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. The friends waiting are an external pressure, not a reason.

questions.q: Which end do you land on?
questions.a: Probably the crosswind end. A 10-knot tailwind adds about 21% to landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]], and a light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution for wake [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Check the crosswind against the airplane and the pilot: about 0.2 VSO is demonstrated [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. The upslope will also shorten the roll [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

questions.q: Your learner is flying a low-wing airplane. After touchdown they reach to retract the flaps to keep mud off them. What do you say?
questions.a: Leave them down. Mud, stones or slush can damage low-wing flaps, but retracting them on the roll is inadvisable because full control of the airplane matters more [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

questions.q: The towplane lands ahead of you. How do you handle wake and traffic?
questions.a: Stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point, if that still leaves firm ground and room for a no-brake roll [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Keep scanning and calling: most midairs happen near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].

questions.q: In the float the airspeed suddenly drops 10 knots and the airplane sinks. What now?
questions.a: Full power and go around, since this may be windshear from the building cumulus [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Don't pitch up below a speed the airplane can climb at, and stay in ground effect until it accelerates [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

questions.q: On the second try, a tight base-to-final turn overshoots. The learner reaches for bottom rudder. Your call, and why?
questions.a: Go around. Skidding turns and steep banks at that height set up a cross-control stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], and 60 percent of stall/spin accidents happen during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. No LAHSO or rush changes that [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing and after-landing checklists while explaining why briefings are done before the approach.
skills.practice: Finish all briefings and checklists except the landing checklist before final, and say why aloud [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Make the pattern radio calls, towered or nontowered, with correct phraseology.
skills.practice: Script downwind, base and final calls with the airport name at both ends [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]] [[33:210|AIM 4-1-9]].

skills.do: Confirm alignment with the correct or assigned runway and explain how you avoid a wrong surface landing.
skills.practice: On every final say the runway number and check it against the plan [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Scan the landing runway and nearby area for traffic and obstructions and point them out to the 'learner'.
skills.practice: Make a spoken scan part of short final; don't let the learner leave it to you [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

skills.do: Pick an aim and touchdown point for the wind, surface and obstructions, and explain why you chose it.
skills.practice: Choose the point from the airplane, the landing type, the conditions and expected performance, not by habit [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

skills.do: Set the recommended configuration, speed and trim and fly a stabilized approach with small pitch and power changes, explaining throttle versus elevator corrections.
skills.practice: Call each deviation as a total energy or distribution error before you correct it [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

skills.do: Maintain manufacturer's published approach airspeed or in its absence not more than 1.3 times the stalling speed or the minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration (VSO), ±5 knots with gust factor applied.
skills.practice: Fly the short-field approach speed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], adding no more than half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]], while talking.

skills.do: Hold directional control and crosswind correction from final through the slow float, touchdown and rollout.
skills.practice: Practice adding aileron and rudder as speed decays in the float [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

skills.do: Make smooth, timely round-out and touchdown inputs with power in, and keep the nose wheel off until loss of elevator effectiveness.
skills.practice: Fly low passes and landings holding the nose up as long as the elevator works [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

skills.do: Touch down at the proper nose-high attitude with minimum sink rate, no side drift, and the longitudinal axis on the runway center.
skills.practice: Use power to set the sink and the upwind main first in a crosswind [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

skills.do: Hold elevator as the manufacturer recommends on the rollout and exit the soft area fast enough not to sink in.
skills.practice: No brakes; lower the nose gently with a touch of power and keep rolling [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

skills.do: Go around on time when the approach is outside the tolerances or anything makes the landing unsafe, and explain the decision.
skills.practice: Brief go-around triggers before each lesson and practice going around from the float [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

skills.do: Taxi on the soft surface with proper control positions and enough speed to keep moving.
skills.practice: Wind control positions plus continuous motion with power [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

skills.do: Watch the examiner make a soft-field error, name it, explain the cause and demonstrate the fix.
skills.practice: Drill the eleven rows of the error table until you can spot each from the right seat [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: Which approach speed does the AFH pair with the soft-field landing?
options: The normal approach speed plus 10 knots
The short-field final-approach speed
VY, for a quick go-around
1.5 VSO in all conditions
quiz.why: The short-field final-approach speed is equally appropriate for soft-field landings [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: Short final, you are high and slow. What kind of energy error is that, and which control fixes it first?
options: Total energy too high; throttle
Total energy too low; throttle
Energy distribution error; elevator
Energy distribution error; throttle
quiz.why: Altitude and speed are off in opposite directions, so total energy is about right and the elevator trades height for speed [[24:98|AFH 4-12]] [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

quiz.q: Why does a little power help the learner flare at very low speed?
options: It keeps the stall warning quiet
It sends more air over the elevator and keeps its authority
It makes the airplane float shorter
It reduces induced drag
quiz.why: A small amount of power gives the elevator more authority at low airspeeds; a windmilling prop can block that airflow [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

quiz.q: S9 asks you to keep the nose wheel off until when?
options: Until the airplane stops
Until loss of elevator effectiveness
Until 10 knots below touchdown speed
Until the flaps are up
quiz.why: ACS AI.VII.D.S9. The AFH short-field text uses the same idea: hold the attitude as long as the elevators remain effective [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

quiz.q: Which runway surface fact is true according to the PHAK?
options: Mud always lengthens the landing
Mud and water reduce friction but can also act as obstructions that shorten the landing
Grass has no effect on landing distance
Performance charts assume a grass surface
quiz.why: Muddy and wet surfaces reduce friction but can also act as obstructions and reduce landing distance [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

quiz.q: During a long soft-field float in a crosswind, what happens to the correction you were holding?
options: It becomes too much
It stays the same
It becomes inadequate as the controls lose effectiveness
It no longer matters once in ground effect
quiz.why: As airspeed decreases the controls become less effective and the correction becomes inadequate, so deflection must increase [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

quiz.q: Who should not take part in LAHSO, according to the AIM?
options: Pilots of tailwheel airplanes
Student pilots and pilots not familiar with LAHSO
Any pilot at a nontowered airport
Pilots flying at night
quiz.why: Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

quiz.q: Why does the AIH warn against heavy coaching on final?
options: It voids the learner's logbook entry
It can reduce collision avoidance and cause missed radio calls
It is forbidden by 14 CFR
It slows the learner's progress to solo
quiz.why: Excessive teaching on final can cost collision avoidance and situational awareness and cause missed transmissions; use concise prompts [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

quiz.q: Which pair of normal-landing habits most often fights the soft-field technique?
options: Checklist use and radio calls
Idle power in the flare and lowering the nose soon after touchdown
Crabbing on base and slipping on final
Using the aim point and the horizon
quiz.why: The soft-field landing keeps power on through touchdown and holds the nose wheel off [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], so old habits transfer negatively [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

quiz.q: Where is the margin of safety smallest in the AIH's Figure 1-14?
options: Preflight
Takeoff
Cruise
Approach and landing
quiz.why: The margin of safety is minimal during the approach and landing [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

final_quiz.q: VSO is 48 knots, the POH lists no approach speed, and the wind is 10 gusting 16. About what airspeed window do you hold on the CFI checkride?
options: About 60 to 70 knots
About 57 to 67 knots
About 63 to 73 knots
About 62 to 77 knots
final_quiz.why: 1.3 x 48 = 62.4, plus no more than half the 6-knot gust factor (3) = 65.4, about 65 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. The CFI standard is ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.D.S7): about 60 to 70.

final_quiz.q: Your learner rounds out about 6 feet up and the airplane seems to stop descending. Speed is still adequate. What do you coach?
options: Push the nose down to get back to the surface
Hold the attitude until it settles, adding a little power if needed
Close the throttle so it sinks
Pull back more to land in the stall attitude now
final_quiz.why: Hold the pitch constant until it starts down again, with a slight amount of power if needed; don't lower the nose that close to the runway without power [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

final_quiz.q: The 'learner' (your examiner) lands on all three wheels fast, then pushes the yoke forward. The airplane starts to swerve. Your correction?
options: Apply firm brakes to stop the swerve
Smooth back-elevator pressure, and go around if runway and conditions permit
More forward pressure for nose-wheel steering
Raise the flaps to kill lift
final_quiz.why: That is wheelbarrowing. It is usually fixed with smooth back-elevator pressure; a prompt go-around is advisable if the runway permits [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

final_quiz.q: On a simulated soft rollout on pavement, your learner brakes 'just a little to make the taxiway.' What is the soft-field reason to stop that habit?
options: Brakes wear out on grass
Braking loads the nose gear and can make the nose wheel dig in
Braking raises the nose
Braking is illegal on turf
final_quiz.why: Brakes are not needed on a soft field and may load the nose gear and make the nose wheel dig in [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner arrives 15 knots fast and floats well past the planned touchdown point on a strip whose firm part is short. Best call?
options: Push the airplane onto the ground
Go around
Close the throttle and brake hard after touchdown
Slip to lose speed in the float
final_quiz.why: Prolonged floating uses a lot of runway; if a landing can't be made in the first third, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. Forcing a floating airplane on can start porpoising [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].

final_quiz.q: In a tailwheel airplane, how should the soft-field touchdown look?
options: Mains first, tail high, then brakes
Tailwheel with or just before the mains, then firm back pressure holding it down
Wheel landing at higher speed to keep the tail flying
Three-point, then forward pressure to keep weight on the mains
final_quiz.why: The tailwheel touches with or just before the mains and is held down with firm back-elevator pressure through the roll [[24:294|AFH 14-8]].

final_quiz.q: A larger airplane is departing the runway you are landing on, a soft-surface runway. Where does the AIM say to land?
options: Beyond its rotation point
Well before its rotation point
At its touchdown point
Anywhere after waiting 1 minute
final_quiz.why: Behind a departing larger aircraft on the same runway, note its rotation point and land well prior to it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

final_quiz.q: At 100 feet on a soft-field final the airplane is low and very slow, near the stall warning. Using the AFH energy grid, what is the right first action?
options: Pull the nose up to stretch to the field
Full throttle and avoid pitching up
Reduce power and dive for speed
Raise the flaps to reduce drag
final_quiz.why: Lower and very slow is the 'dangerous' box: apply full throttle and avoid pitching up on the backside of the power curve [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

final_quiz.q: On the first soft-field lesson, you ask the learner to make the CTAF call during the float, and the landing falls apart. Best explanation?
options: They lack radio skill
In the early stage, performing takes all their attention and distractions make it deteriorate
They need a longer briefing in the air
They are at a learning plateau
final_quiz.why: In the cognitive stage, performing a skill takes all the learner's attention and instructor distractions often make it deteriorate [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: While practicing soft-field landings, the airplane sinks hard in the float and both you and the learner reach for the throttle. What brief would have prevented this?
options: A briefing on flap speeds
Agreeing who has complete control of the throttle
A longer final approach
Brakes check before landing
final_quiz.why: For simulated emergency landings the AFH says either the instructor or the pilot should have complete control of the throttle [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. The same clarity applies to soft-field practice.

final_quiz.q: You load the airplane 10% heavier than on the last turf landing. What does the PHAK predict?
options: About 10% faster landing speed and 21% longer distance
About 5% faster landing speed and 10% longer distance
No change; indicated speed is the same
About 16% longer distance
final_quiz.why: A 10% weight increase gives about a 5% increase in landing velocity and a 10% increase in landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your school trains on a 6,000-foot paved runway with no grass strip nearby. How can you add soft-field factors without more flight time?
options: Skip them until the learner owns an airplane
Discuss runway conditions, short strips, high weight and density altitude on the ground as a layered scenario
Send the learner solo to find a grass strip
Teach only the checkride tolerances
final_quiz.why: The AIH's Phase II adds runway conditions and other factors through ground discussion of a harder scenario, with no added flight training [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says a firm soft-field touchdown 'is no big deal, the tires absorb it.' What AFH fact answers that?
options: Tires absorb all of it below 300 fpm
A 6-inch drop is about 340 fpm and touchdown loads can reach three to four times the airplane's weight
Only the nose gear carries landing loads
Grass halves the touchdown load
final_quiz.why: A 6-inch free fall is roughly a 340 fpm descent, and the load at touchdown may be three or four times the airplane's weight [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

takeaways: Hold the short-field approach speed ±5 knots and explain it as you fly; extra speed only floats [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Power stays in through touchdown: pitch holds the attitude, power sets the sink and the weight transfer [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Nose wheel off until the elevator stops working, then lowered gently with a touch of power; no brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Low and slow is a throttle problem; high and slow or low and fast is an elevator problem [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Expect the normal-landing habits to come back and plan to catch them [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].
Simulate safely: name the soft part, brief go-around triggers and who has the throttle, and keep coaching short on final.
Pick strips with honest personal minimums, and look before you land [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
cfi_notes: The AFH stabilized-approach list allows +10/-5 knots [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], and so does the private ACS. Your standard is ±5 (ACS AI.VII.D.S7). Train to the tighter number in your own flying.

The AFH says to close the throttle right after touchdown in its 'use of power' and ballooning notes [[24:202|AFH 9-31]] [[24:204|AFH 9-33]], but the soft-field section uses power after touchdown to control weight transfer and to keep moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Point out the difference; it is where the 'chop it' habit comes from.

The AFH calls the soft-field approach 'similar to the normal approach' [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] and then says to use the short-field approach speed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. Learners who hear 'normal' fly normal speed and float. Stress the speed.

The ACS phrase 'until loss of elevator effectiveness' is not in the AFH soft-field section. The short-field section says to hold the attitude as long as the elevators remain effective [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Teach them as one picture.
The AFH lists soft-field errors but not their fixes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. The fixes in this lesson come from the surrounding AFH text on faulty landings; say so if a learner asks where they come from.
PHAK 11-17 gives 'at least 21 percent' and '20 percent' for 10 percent excess landing speed on the same page [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Either shows the idea.
The AIH's three-phase example is short-field landings [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]. Using it for soft-field landings is an application, but a close one.
Most checkrides are on pavement, so the examiner will evaluate S11 and S13 as a simulation and probe them orally. Have your 'soft area ends at the second taxiway' callout and exit plan ready.
In a low-wing airplane mud, stones or slush can damage the flaps, yet flaps are still recommended [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. Use the POH; don't let a learner retract them on the roll to protect them.
gaps: No source gives a procedure, minimum altitude or runway length for simulating a soft field on pavement or for practice low passes in ground effect. Use your school's SOP.
Power setting in the float, flap setting and grass or wet-grass landing corrections are airplane-specific: POH/AFM.
No source gives the airspeed at which elevator effectiveness is lost; it depends on the airplane, CG and power.

S11 and S13 call for manufacturer-recommended elevator and 'proper' control positions on a soft surface. The sources give wind control positions [[24:56|AFH 2-19]] and the keep-moving rule [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], not a back-elevator position for taxiing a nosewheel airplane in mud.
No source gives landing distance factors for wet grass, mud or snow; the PHAK only says soft ground has a significant effect [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

activities.title: Throttle, elevator, or both?
activities.intro: Each card is a deviation on final. Tap it, then tap the control that fixes it first, using the AFH energy rules.

activities.title: Read the balloon
activities.intro: Drag each name to its pin.

pins.label: Round out begins near the surface
Nose raised too fast: climbing, speed decaying

activities.title: From short final to firm ground
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put your demonstration in order, then tap Check.
steps: Stabilized at the short-field approach speed
Round out and leave some power in
Fly 1 to 2 feet up while speed bleeds off
Touch down nose-high at the lowest speed
Hold the nose wheel off with back pressure
Once committed, ease the nose wheel down with a touch of power
Keep rolling to firm ground, no brakes

activities.title: Soft-field numbers
activities.intro: Work each one from the lesson's rules, then type your answer.

items.q: No POH approach speed, VSO 50 knots, wind 10 gusting 18. Highest target approach speed?
items.why: 1.3 x 50 = 65, plus half the 8-knot gust factor (4) = 69 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

items.q: POH landing distance is 1,200 feet in calm wind. About how far with a 10-knot tailwind?
items.why: A 10-knot tailwind adds about 21% [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]: 1,200 x 1.21 = 1,452 feet.

items.q: Minimum landing distance is 1,000 feet at sea level. About how far at 5,000 feet, same weight?
items.why: At 5,000 feet minimum landing distance is 16% greater [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]: 1,000 x 1.16 = 1,160 feet.

items.q: A landing takes 1,500 feet. About how far if you are 10% heavier?
items.why: 10% more weight gives about 10% more landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]: 1,500 x 1.10 = 1,650 feet.

items.q: A pilot's shortest-runway minimum is 2,500 feet. What is it for an unfamiliar turf strip, using the RMH adjustment?
items.why: Add at least 500 feet for unfamiliar airports [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]: 2,500 + 500 = 3,000 feet.

activities.title: True or false: going around and holding short
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Once you accept a LAHSO clearance, you may no longer reject the landing.
cards.why: False. A LAHSO clearance does not preclude a rejected landing [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

cards.s: Pilots should only receive a LAHSO clearance with at least a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility.
The cushion of air in ground effect lets you climb out early in a go-around from the float.
cards.why: False. The cushion is imaginary; the performance is borrowed and climbing out early may leave the airplane unable to climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

cards.s: Raising all the flaps at once in a go-around can settle the airplane onto the ground.
cards.why: True. Retract them in small increments [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: The AFH names landing expectancy and pride as the two sources of go-around delay.
After a larger aircraft's touch-and-go, the AIM says one minute is enough before you land.

activities.title: Your learner's first soft-field landings
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your learner flies good normal and short-field landings. Today you introduce the soft-field landing on a long paved runway. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: On the ground, which brief fits this lesson best?
options: Only the ACS speed tolerance
Power stays in, nose up after touchdown, no brakes, the 'soft' part of the runway, go-around triggers, and who has the throttle
A full aerodynamics lecture on ground effect in the airplane
Nothing; let the learner discover it
steps.why: Teach before contacting the tower, not during the landing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]], and agree who has the throttle [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]. The content is the soft-field differences [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

steps.s: Short final, the learner is 8 knots fast. What do you say?
options: A long explanation of ground effect
A short prompt: 'Speed,' and let them fix it
Nothing, the float will sort it out
Take the controls
steps.why: Use concise prompting on final [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Extra speed means excessive float [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], so it matters.

steps.s: In the float the learner closes the throttle and the airplane starts to sink fast, 3 feet up. Best action?
options: Say nothing and debrief later
Prompt 'power' or add a little yourself to cushion, and go around if it can't be saved
Push the nose down
Pull full back right away
steps.why: Power cushions a sink and keeps the elevator effective [[24:202|AFH 9-31]] [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]; go around if the landing is uncertain [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

steps.s: On the next landing the nose wheel drops right after touchdown. What do you find out first?
options: Whether they forgot the procedure or an old habit took over: ask them to tell you what they did
Their logbook hours
Whether the tires are worn
Nothing; repeat until it works
steps.why: Teach from what actually happened on that approach, not mechanically [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. An old normal-landing habit is negative transfer [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

steps.s: After eight tries the learner is stuck and frustrated. What now?
options: Ten more soft-field landings
Move to another task and come back later
End training for the month
Lower the standard
steps.why: A plateau is normal; over-practice can cause it, and a break to another place in the curriculum helps [[25:77|AIH 3-26]].
